column4: Following 78:21's Hell as a مِرْصاد (the section's source dictionary form under ر ص د), this ayah identifies the transgressors as those whose return is there; it names the people who meet the watchpoint.
The section says travelers learn of the watcher when the blow falls; this ayah recalls towns destroyed when punishment came at night or while their people slept, a direct scene of an unseen strike.

The section's dictionary gloss for ج و ب includes cutting across countries; this ayah says earlier, stronger peoples traversed the lands but found no place of escape, joining the route to the failure to outrun judgment.

After 50:36 describes powerful generations searching the lands without escape, this ayah says the account is a reminder for a heart or an attentive listener, distinguishing travel from seeing with insight as in the section's source root رءي.

The section names Pharaoh among rulers who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says he exalted himself in the land, divided its people, and was among the corrupters, making the transgression concrete.
The section's source root ط غ ي names crossing a limit; Moses and Aaron are told to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, repeating the section's diagnosis of the ruler.
The section names Pharaoh among those who overstepped in the lands; Moses is told to go to him because he has transgressed, a second direct formulation of the same warning.
The section asks the listener to see what God did to earlier tyrants; this ayah says God seized Pharaoh with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life, giving the ruler's end as an example.
The section makes a past ruler's fate a sight for the listener; this ayah calls Pharaoh's seizure a lesson for whoever fears, making the intended stance explicit.
The section describes the human who reads abundance as honor; Pharaoh points to Egypt's kingdom and rivers flowing beneath him as proof of his standing, joining wealth, land, and self-estimation.
The section's human takes material ease as a verdict of honor; Pharaoh calls Moses contemptible and cites his lack of eloquence, exposing a ruler's false measure of worth.
The section names Thamud among the peoples made visible to the listener; this ayah says Thamud denied the warnings, setting up their own account of overstepping and punishment.
The section links passage through the land to the fate of Thamud; this ayah says their she-camel is sent as a test for them, making their response to a divinely set limit the central scene.
The section develops a watchpoint where every traveler must pass; this ayah assigns the camel and the people their separate turns at the water, a concrete boundary they must observe.
The section describes a sudden blow following transgression; this ayah says the people called their companion, who seized the camel and hamstrung it, the act that brings the punishment.
The section places the blow before the watchpoint is named; this ayah says a single cry was sent against Thamud and they became like dry stalks, completing the consequence of the broken limit.
The section's human reads plenty as honor and scarcity as humiliation; this ayah offers the example of a secure town given abundant provision, then made to taste hunger and fear after ingratitude.
The section's human judges honor by ample provision; this ayah calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life but says enduring good deeds are better with the Lord, replacing that measure.
The section's human reads a favorable worldly condition as honor; this ayah says earthly adornment is a test of who acts best, directly naming the purpose of visible plenty.
After 18:7 calls earthly adornment a test, this ayah says the earth will be made barren ground, showing what remains when the visible provision passes.

The section joins crossing the lands with people who mistake status for security; this ayah tells believers not to be deceived by the disbelievers' movement through the land, making their apparent power a false sign.
After 3:196 warns against being impressed by the disbelievers' movement, this ayah calls their enjoyment brief and their destination Hell, separating worldly ease from final honor.
The section's person reads what he has been given as honor; this ayah says worldly provision and adornment are temporary and what is with God is better and more lasting.
After 28:60 contrasts worldly provision with what lasts, this ayah asks whether the one promised a good outcome is like the one merely enjoying worldly life before being brought to judgment.

The section shows provision being misread as personal rank; this ayah tells Qarun to use what God gave him for the Hereafter and not to seek corruption in the land, giving the right response to abundance.

The section names those who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says the Hereafter's home is for those who do not seek exaltation or corruption on earth, marking the boundary opposite their overreach.
The section's human ranks himself by present ease; this ayah says people prefer the nearer life, naming the preference that turns temporary provision into their measure.
After 87:16 names preference for the nearer life, this ayah says the Hereafter is better and more enduring, supplying the comparison that the section's human overlooks.
The section names those who crossed their limits in the lands; this ayah says the one who transgressed is among those whose end is being described.
After 79:37 identifies the transgressor, this ayah says he preferred worldly life, making that preference the particular inward choice behind the outcome.
After the transgressor prefers worldly life in 79:38, this ayah names Hell as his refuge, reversing the security he thought his status gave him.
The section's human makes a judgment from worldly conditions; this ayah contrasts him with the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire.
Following the restraint in 79:40, this ayah says the Garden is that person's refuge, giving the enduring outcome opposite the worldly preference.

The section says the human judges by how much provision he has; this ayah describes the one who withholds and sees himself as self-sufficient (اسْتَغْنَىٰ), a close parallel to 96:7 and the section's mistaken gaze.
After describing the self-sufficient person in 92:8, this ayah says he denies the best outcome, connecting his self-estimation to his failure to heed the warning.
After the person withholds and denies, this ayah says he will be eased toward hardship, reversing the assumption that present ease signals honor.
This continuation says his wealth will not avail him when he falls, directly undoing the section's human claim that provision is his honor.
The section contrasts a human's reading of present provision with his final state; this ayah describes the believer who seeks the Hereafter and strives for it, giving the other orientation to life.
After distinguishing those who seek the Hereafter in 17:19, this ayah says God provides to both groups from His gift, showing that worldly provision alone does not mark approval.
This ayah asks the reader to look at how some are favored over others in worldly life, then says the Hereafter has greater degrees and preference, directly correcting the section's status judgment.
The section joins human communities spread through the lands with provision as a test; this ayah says people were divided into nations across the earth and tested with good and bad things.

The section says provision and restriction are a test; this ayah explicitly names fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives, and fruits as tests, including the scarcity that the human misreads as humiliation.
After 2:155 names losses as a test, this ayah gives the response of those who say they belong to God and return to Him, rather than calling the test humiliation.
The section makes human provision an ordeal misread as a verdict; this ayah says people will be tested in their wealth and lives, making the trial explicit.
Before 72:9's flame waiting for a listener, this ayah reports that the jinn found the sky filled with strong guards and flames, establishing the guarded passage that the section invokes.
After the jinn encounter the waiting flame in 72:9, this ayah records their uncertainty about whether harm or right guidance is intended for people, completing their response to the changed watch.
Following Lot's night-escape command in 15:65, this ayah tells him the people will be cut off in the morning, setting the dangerous passage against the fate awaiting those left behind.
After Moses is told to leave at night in 44:23, this ayah tells him to leave the sea open because Pharaoh's host will drown in it, turning the route to safety into the pursuer's trap.

The section's night travelers pass along a route while the watcher waits; this ayah says Pharaoh pursued the Israelites across the sea until drowning caught him, reversing the roles of pursued and pursuer.
The section's watcher attends to what every person does; this ayah says the record is set out and leaves nothing small or great uncounted, making the hidden record visible at judgment.
The section says people fail to see the watcher before the strike; this ayah says they did not hide their hearing, eyes, and skins because they thought God did not know much of what they did.
After 41:22 exposes their assumption that God did not know, this ayah says that very thought ruined them, naming the cost of misreading the unseen watcher.

The section extends the watch from the road to every spoken word; this ayah asks whether people think God does not hear their secrets and private conversations, then says messengers are present recording them.

The section's human misjudges provision as honor or humiliation; this ayah says just scales will be set on the Day of Resurrection and no soul will be wronged, giving a measured judgment that does not follow worldly appearance.

The section says the traveler learns of the watcher when the blow falls; this ayah says people were given everything and rejoiced, then were seized suddenly after forgetting the warning, a direct account of false security under abundance.
The section's watcher waits where people do not perceive him; this ayah says those who deny the signs will be drawn on gradually from where they do not know.
After 7:182 describes the gradual approach unseen, this ayah says respite is given while God's plan is firm, explaining how security can conceal the approaching judgment.
After 41:12, this ayah warns that if people turn away they will face a thunderbolt like that of ʿĀd and Thamud, directly bringing the section's named peoples into a warning before judgment.

The section's wording about guards before and behind the messenger (72:27) describes protective watch; here the phrase for messengers coming from before and behind describes repeated warnings across generations, not guards stationed around one messenger.
The section recalls what happened to Thamud after their boundary-breaking; this ayah says an earthquake seized them and they lay dead in their homes, another account of the sudden end.
Following the secure, well-provided town's punishment in 16:112, this ayah says a messenger came from among them but they denied him, identifying the refusal behind the change from provision to fear.
The section gives مَثَل the secondary sense of an instructive lesson; this ayah says every kind of example has been presented in the Qur'an, yet most people persist in disbelief.

The section's source dictionary connects مَثَل with a lesson; this ayah says examples are set out for people, but disbelievers reject the sign, matching the failure to see a lesson in the section's history.

The section's source dictionary joins the image (مِثال) with seeing and the lesson (مَثَل); this ayah's parable of a person lighting a fire ends with his light taken away and his inability to see, combining the image's two senses.
The section's source dictionary gives مَثَل the sense of lesson; this ayah compares worldly life to rain-fed growth that becomes dry debris, a concrete image of provision that passes.

The section's human reads worldly abundance as honor; this ayah describes worldly life as adornment, boasting, and competition in wealth and children, then compares its growth to vegetation that withers.
The section names those who exceeded limits in the lands; this ayah depicts a boundary between two seas that they do not cross, a specific reversal in which a limit is kept.
